extracted.intended_audience: editors and scholars of poetry / textual critics working with early printed editions and manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Deciding between variant readings in poetic texts and preparing an edition: choose readings and record variants using principles of metre, rhyme, manuscript authority, sense, scribal error, and philological knowledge. Produce an apparatus of various readings and note uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve metrical integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the reading which preserves the poem's metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aldus's reading ever would was rejected because 'as this would hurt the Metre, we have restored it to its genuine Reading, by observing that Synæresis which had been neglected by ignorant Transcribers.' Apply knowledge of metrical phenomena (e.g. synæresis) when preferring one variant over another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight manuscript and editorial authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Give consideration to how many and which manuscripts or editions support a variant; prefer readings supported by strong authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For 'hourly' versus 'daily' or 'nightly' the editor notes 'the last has great Authorities of its side.' For numerals, 'so many of them concur in this last reading, that I am very much in doubt whether it ought not to take place.' Balance quantity and quality of witnesses when choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect rhyme constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer variants that fit the poem's rhyme scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The German manuscript's 'a lasting Passion' was rejected because 'the Rhyme will not admit it.' The editor also preferred 'in one' over 'in two' partly 'because the Rhime... is preserved by it.' Rhyme can trump variant readings unless there is compelling contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obvious scribal/transcription errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject readings that are likely the result of mechanical mistakes by transcribers (misreading letters, punctuation, or numerals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Vatican manuscript's reading of 'it' for 'I' is attributed to a transcriber mistaking 'the Dash of the I for a T'; numerals can be corrupted by omitted cyphers or mistaken dashes ('a Hundred' vs 'a Thousand'). Prefer readings that correct such likely errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external/contextual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose readings consistent with a poem's context, usage in other authors, or known referents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Several manuscripts read 'his' Wit or 'your' Wit, but the editor chooses 'her' because 'I find Corinna to be the Name of a Woman in other Authors.' External literary evidence can resolve pronoun/gender variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about emendation; favour manuscript consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not alter names or words based on etymological speculation alone when the manuscript tradition supports the received reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The editor resists changing 'Belvidera' into 'Pelvidera' despite an etymological argument, noting 'Did not all the Manuscripts reclaim, I should change Belvidera into Pelvidera' — but because manuscripts support Belvidera, he does not emend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider rhetorical effect and authorial taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When readings differ, prefer the variant that better fits the poet's likely rhetorical intent or taste (e.g., stronger compliment, more fitting diction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The editor prefers 'Thousand' to 'a Hundred' because 'the Word _Thousand_ was ten Times a greater Compliment to the Poet's Mistress than an _Hundred_.' Consider authorial praise and rhetorical force when weighing variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain the usual/established reading absent strong cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an alternative reading exists but the customary reading is defensible, stick to the usual reading unless there is a clear reason to prefer otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For 'the fatal Stroke' some editors read 'a', yet the editor 'has stuck to the usual Reading.' Respect editorial tradition unless contradicted by metre, manuscript authority, or sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply philological and orthographic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Use knowledge of historical orthography, contractions, and poetic pronunciation (e.g., synæresis, ampersand forms) to interpret variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Note that '&' may appear as three distinct letters in some manuscripts; apply synæresis to restore metre; explain orthographic differences as possible causes of variant readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish an apparatus of various readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide readers with the several variant readings from former editions and ancient manuscripts alongside the chosen text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening statement: the Ode is presented 'in a new Edition, with the several various Readings which I find of it in former Editions, and in Ancient Manuscripts.' Include notes that give the surrounding explanation and examples to justify editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainty and defer when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is inconclusive, openly record uncertainty and leave difficult questions to learned readers or future scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: On the 'in two' / 'in one' variant the editor concludes 'But this I shall leave to the Learned, without determining any thing in a Matter of so great Uncertainty.' Explicitly note unresolved problems rather than forcing a dubious emendation.
